title: The Man Who Ran Before the News
paragraphs:
The Man Who Ran Before the News
The Untold Story of the Messenger Running Ahead of Absalom’s News
There are moments in Scripture that seem so small we almost run past them.
Then he disappears from the biblical narrative forever.

Yet hidden inside one brief moment during one of Israel's darkest family tragedies is a lesson that speaks directly into modern hearts obsessed with recognition, platforms, influence, visibility, and applause.
The story unfolds in the shadow of betrayal, rebellion, heartbreak, and a father's shattered soul.
And at the center of it all is a man most Christians have never noticed.
A man who arrived before the news.
And perhaps, without realizing it, a picture of every believer called to carry the message of a King.
The account is found during the rebellion of Absalom against his father, King David.
Absalom was not merely a rebellious son.
He was a son who stole hearts.
"Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." (2 Samuel 15:6)
The Hebrew word used for "stole" is לָקַח (laqach), carrying the sense of taking, seizing, or capturing.
Absalom did not simply gain popularity.
He captured loyalty that belonged to another.
He took hearts that should have remained devoted to the king.
David's own son became his enemy.
The rebellion exploded into civil war.
And David carried a burden few parents can understand.
When the battle finally came, David gave a strange command.
"Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom." (2 Samuel 18:5)
But he wanted mercy even more.
The father still loved the son who had tried to destroy him.
Long before the cross, another shadow of grace was already appearing.
Because this is how God loves rebels.
This is how God loves sinners.
This is how God loves us.
Yet His heart still runs after us.
Someone had to carry news that would simultaneously save a kingdom and break a father's heart.
The first messenger selected was a Cushite servant.
He was entrusted with the truth.
The son of Zadok the priest.
Again and again he pleaded for permission.
"You shall not take the news this day." (2 Samuel 18:20)
Joab understood something many modern believers forget.
Not everyone who wants to carry a message is prepared for the weight of that message.
"Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite." (2 Samuel 18:23)
Yet he did not carry the complete message.
But he carried what David truly needed to hear.
The faster runner was not the fuller messenger.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully relevant.
But heaven has never been impressed by who arrives first.
Heaven cares about who faithfully carries the King's message.
Some believers spend their lives trying to outrun everyone else.
Yet the Kingdom has never been built by the fastest runners.
It has always been built by faithful messengers.
Jesus never commanded His disciples to become famous.
He commanded them to become faithful.
The Greek word translated "faithful" throughout the New Testament is πιστός (pistos).
One who can be trusted with what belongs to another.
That is the heart of biblical success.
One day every earthly platform will disappear.
Every human achievement will be forgotten.
The tragedy of modern Christianity is that many want the influence of Ahimaaz but not the responsibility of carrying truth.
We want to be seen running.
We want people to notice our effort.
We want recognition for our activity.
But the Kingdom is not advanced by appearances.
The most powerful servants of God are often the least visible.
The mother teaching Scripture to her children.
The father quietly leading his family.
The disciple sharing Christ without cameras.
The saint whose name never trends but whose faithfulness shakes eternity.
David's story also reveals another deeper Gospel reality.
When news finally reached him, the victorious king did not celebrate.
The Scripture records one of the most heartbreaking cries in the Bible:
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would God I had died for thee." (2 Samuel 18:33)
David wanted to die in Absalom's place.
A human king could wish it.
Only the King of Kings could accomplish it.
David's cry points forward to another King.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ did what David could never do.
The Son of God actually died for rebels.
Actually died for those who stole their hearts away from their rightful King.
The Gospel is not the story of good people finding God.
It is the story of a holy King pursuing rebels who deserve judgment and offering grace through His Son.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), translated "grace," means undeserved favor.
A gift that cannot be purchased.
A blessing that cannot be deserved.
Every believer was once an Absalom.
Every believer stole loyalty from God.
Yet Christ stepped into our place.
The cross became the meeting point of justice and mercy.
The place where scandal became grace.
The place where broken stories were rewritten forever.
That is why this forgotten messenger matters.
Because his story asks a question every believer must answer.
Or are you carrying the King's message?
Those are not always the same thing.
And when eternity finally arrives, nobody will care who ran fastest.
Everyone will care who carried the truth.
The Lord sees every faithful step.
Nothing done for Christ is ever wasted.
Nothing surrendered to Christ is ever lost.
Nothing entrusted to Christ remains unchanged.
Because that is what Jesus does.
He takes rebels and makes them sons.
He takes shame and creates testimony.
He takes ruins and builds redemption.
He takes scandal and turns it into grace.
And He is still rewriting stories today.
If this message stirred something in your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Have you ever felt forgotten while trying to remain faithful to God?
Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
Because one faithful step in obedience may matter more in eternity than a lifetime spent chasing applause.
